planting.note: Plant divisions or container specimens in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; bamboo iris forms upright, cane-like stems with fans of leaves similar to I. japonica but taller, and spreads by rhizomes to form open clumps.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; bamboo iris is a crested (Lophiris group) species closely related to Iris japonica, producing tall, cane-like, bamboo-reminiscent stems clothed in fans of broad evergreen leaves, topped in spring by clusters of flattened, orchid-like pale lavender to white flowers marked with orange-yellow crests. It is somewhat taller and more upright than the stoloniferous I. japonica, making it useful as a textural accent at the back of a shaded border or along a woodland path under high canopy. Protect from hard freezes in marginal zones, as foliage and stems are more tender than many other crested irises. Divide congested clumps in spring as new growth begins.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container specimens in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; this crested iris produces tall, stiff, cane-like stems and needs shelter from hard frost and strong wind.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; Wattii iris is a large, evergreen crested (Lophiris group) species native to woodland margins of southern China and the Himalayan foothills, forming tall, bamboo-like canes topped with broad fans of glossy leaves. In spring it bears abundant, flattened, pale blue-violet flowers marked with deeper violet and gold crests, held above the foliage on branching stems. It favors the same dappled woodland conditions as Iris japonica and Iris confusa but grows noticeably taller, making it a striking accent for a sheltered shade garden or conservatory border in frost-free to mild climates. Protect from freezing temperatures, which damage the evergreen canes.

planting.note: Plant divisions in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to light partial shade; Japanese iris are heavy water users and perform best at a pond margin or in a bog-like bed that never fully dries out.

directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to light partial shade. Flying Tiger, a Japanese iris bred by American hybridizers Marty Schafer and Jan Sacks, produces flowers heavily streaked and mottled with contrasting color over a paler ground, giving each bloom an irregular, tiger-striped pattern distinct from the more evenly patterned cultivars already in this dataset. Japanese iris demand consistently moist, acidic soil through the growing season and decline quickly if allowed to dry out; a pond margin or heavily irrigated bed suits them best. Divide clumps every three to four years in early fall to maintain vigor and bloom quality.
